Learning Objectives
Differentiate sources of posterior heel pain secondary to Achilles tendon pathology location.
List physical examination features specific to various Achilles tendon pathology.
Determine appropriate imaging modalities and the features of Achilles tendon pathology.
Review nonsurgical treatment options for the management of Achilles tendon pathology.
Discuss intraoperative treatment algorithms for isolated insertional Achilles tendon pathology
and midsubstance tendon Achilles tendinopathy.

Etiology
A retrocalcaneal exostosis, or more commonly referred to as a pump bump
Occurs with rubbing of the shoe with prominence of the posterior calcaneus
Occurs in middle-aged females more than males
Often bilateral
Physical Examination
• A bony prominence (Haglund lesion) at the posterosuperior aspect of the calcaneal tuberosity
• Posterior swelling at the calcaneal bursae

Physical Examination
Haglund exostosis becomes symptomatic if patients have inflammation of the bursa
separating the tendon and the posterior calcaneus wall. Often, this is associated with
wearing constrictive shoes or repetitive activities that involve considerable ankle
dorsiflexion, such as running uphill.1 Pain on physical examination is localized primarily
to the lateral aspect of the calcaneal tuberosity.
Imaging Studies
Lateral foot radiographs: enlargement of the posterosuperior corner of the calcaneus (Figure
1)

posterosuperior calcaneus. (Courtesy of Bethany Gallagher, MD, FAAOS, Nashville, TN.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
3/8-inch heel lift in a shoe or removable boot
Physical therapy
Anti-inflammatory medications (topical and oral)
Surgical Management
Retrocalcaneal bursae decompression and calcaneal ostectomy
Complications
Achilles tendon avulsion
Persistent posterior heel pain
Wound breakdown
Nerve injuries
Medial calcaneal sensory nerve
Sural nerve


Management
Symptoms from a Haglund deformity often are responsive to nonsurgical management,
including shoe wear modifications, such as backless shoes or heel lifts, and activity
restrictions.2 A very limited (to nonexistent) role exists for corticosteroid injections in this
setting; however, an inherent risk of tendon rupture exists because the bursa is
connected to the Achilles tendon peritenon in some individuals. Intratendinous
injections in animal studies suggest that rupture may be a potential complication for
several weeks after injection.3 Physical therapy is beneficial and must include eccentric
strengthening exercises for promotion of tendon health, vascularity, and repair.4
If nonsurgical management is unsuccessful, surgical management is considered. Initial
surgical management includes calcaneoplasty with or without tendon débridement.
Calcaneoplasty can be successfully performed via an open or arthroscopic approach.
Regardless of the surgical approach, the goal is to remove enough bone to prevent
tendon impingement (Figure 2). An arthroscopic surgical procedure is more technically
demanding and cannot adequately address any substantial Achilles tendon pathology
requiring repair;5 however, arthroscopic excision is associated with better outcomes,
such as less postoperative pain, compared with open excision in patients who have an
isolated Haglund deformity without considerable tendinopathy.6
Figure 2 Intraoperative fluoroscopic image of a calcaneus shows bone excision during

Insertional Calcifications and Chronic Insertional Achilles Tendinosis
Etiology
Repetitive overuse trauma resulting in bony change of the posterior calcaneus
Often occurs in patients with retrocalcaneal bursitis and associated Haglund deformity
Physical Examination
Prominence over the insertion of the Achilles tendon with tenderness to palpation
May have associated thickening of the distal Achilles tendon
Often associated with gastrocnemius contracture
Imaging Studies
Lateral foot radiograph: talon-type bone spur at the Achilles tendon insertion and insertional
calcifications (Figure 3)
Figure 3 Lateral foot radiograph demonstrates calcifications within the tendon substance and
at the insertion of the Achilles tendon. (Courtesy of Bethany Gallagher, MD, FAAOS, Nashville,
TN.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000596
5/25

MRI
Intrasubstance tendon degeneration
Partial insertional tears
Proximal tendon pathology
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Appropriate imaging studies aid in surgical planning. Lateral radiographs demonstrate
the magnitude of calcaneal deformity and the extent of calcifications (Figure 3).
Calcifications of the tendon insertion are observed in 73% of patients.7 MRI is the
primary advanced imaging modality used to evaluate insertional Achilles tendon
pathology. Calcaneal edema is observed exclusively in symptomatic patients, and the
extent of degeneration of the tendon observed on MRIs is a predictor of the success of
nonsurgical management.2 MRI may reveal insertional tears, chronic mucoid
degeneration of the tendon insertion, and edema with the tendon and calcaneal
insertion (Figure 4). This imaging modality also may show the proximal extent of tendon
pathology, which is important for surgical planning. Ultrasonography is another option
for imaging but is less specific than MRI in evaluating the tendon-bone interface.

calcaneus and insertional Achilles tendon degenerative changes, with an undersurface
partial-thickness tear. (Courtesy of Bethany Gallagher, MD, FAAOS, Nashville, TN.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Immobilization incorporating heel lifts for plantar flexion
Physical therapy
Eccentric strengthening exercises
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy
Surgical Management
Posterior tendon-splitting approach
Excision of bony calcaneal prominence and intrasubstance tendon calcifications/degeneration
For substantial defects after excision, V-Y advancement or central turndown may be
required.
For defects larger than 50% of the remaining tendon, flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tendon
transfer is indicated


Management
Initially, nonsurgical management of insertional Achilles tendon pain should be
considered. NSAIDs and activity modifications most often are effective.8 Bracing and
immobilization may be effective but require prolonged wear time. Eccentric
strengthening exercises may have a role in management but result in better outcomes in
patients with non-insertional Achilles tendon pathology.9,10 Extracorporeal shockwave
therapy also may be a useful tool in promoting vascularity and angiogenesis at the
Achilles tendon insertion.11,12 Compared with eccentric strengthening exercises,
extracorporeal shockwave therapy has been shown to result in a 64% improvement
compared with the 24% improvement noted with an exercise regimen in isolation.13
If a 6- to 12-month course of nonsurgical treatment fails to improve a patient’s
symptoms, surgical treatment may be considered. Various incisions can be used to
expose the Achilles tendon insertion: medial, lateral, and central. No current studies
show improved outcomes with one incision over another. After the tendon is exposed, a
posterior central split is used to elevate medially and laterally off the calcaneal insertion
(Figure 5). This affords adequate exposure for excision of insertional spurring, Haglund
deformity, and intrasubstance calcifications (Figure 6). Thorough excision of the
diseased tendon and calcifications is required for improved patient outcomes. This may
result in an insertional defect.

(Courtesy of Bethany Gallagher, MD, FAAOS, Nashville, TN.)

Nashville, TN.)
For defects that involve greater than 50% of the tendon width, FHL transfer is
recommended and may improve plantar flexion strength. For this specific defect, the
FHL tendon can be harvested via the same incision. The FHL is associated with limited
donor morbidity, has muscle pull similar to that of the Achilles tendon in gait phase, and
improves the local vascular environment with the low-lying muscle belly.16 The fascia of
the FHL is incised, and the tendon is followed as it passes behind the talus
posteromedially. The FHL is harvested at this level and inserted directly into the
calcaneal tuberosity just anterior to the Achilles tendon. An appropriately sized tunnel is
drilled through the calcaneus, and the tendon is passed through and tensioned in
plantar flexion (Video 1) (Figure 9). It often is secured with the use of biotenodesis
screws and sewn to the diminished Achilles tendon; however, if the insertional defect is
large (>4 cm), more length is required from the FHL tendon. The FHL is harvested in the
medial foot and pulled into the posterior incision. It can then be woven through the
calcaneus and up through the proximal limb to re-create tendon continuity. Good results
after surgical repair of symptomatic insertional Achilles tendinitis are observed in 75% to
91% of patients.17,18

Insertional Achilles tendon surgical complications include insertional rupture and wound
complications. An overall surgical complication rate of approximately 5% is observed
with insertional repair. These complications may range from surgical site hypersensitivity
and painful scarring to considerable wound complications (Figure 10). Achilles tendon
rupture has been reported but often is secondary to a postoperative fall.2

Midsubstance Achilles Tendon Pathology
Classification
Peritendinitis
Isolated inflammation within the peritenon
Peritendinitis with tendinosis
Acute inflammation within the peritenon and associated intrasubstance tendon changes
Tendinosis
Pathophysiology
Chronic degenerative changes within the tendon
Secondary to prolonged acute tendinitis
Decreased vascularity
Repetitive microtrauma
Occurs 2 to 6 cm proximal to the insertion
Patient risk factors
Occurs in males more than females
Hypertension
Obesity
Steroid use

Pathophysiology
Patients with Achilles tendinopathy may have comorbidities, such as gout, seronegative
spondyloarthropathies, sarcoidosis, and hypercholesterolemia.19 In addition, the use of
fluoroquinolone antibiotic agents may lead to tendinopathy; however, it often is self-
limiting. Those with isolated peritendinitis often are younger and more active.

Physical Examination
Peritendinitis
Diffuse posterior swelling
Tenderness along the Achilles tendon with crepitus
Tendinosis
Nodular thickening with the tendon substance
Pain localized over the swollen area
Imaging Studies
Lateral ankle radiograph: calcaneal deformity/Haglund deformity, insertional spurs, and
intrasubstance calcifications in the Achilles tendon
MRI
Axial: loss of Achilles tendon contour and shows percentage of tendon involvement
Sagittal: shows length of involvement

Imaging Studies
MRI is an important imaging modality for evaluation of tendinosis and treatment
planning. MRI allows for clear measurements of the pathology and shows mucoid
degeneration and intrasubstance tears, indicating chronic tendinopathy (Figure 11).
Ultrasonography also can be performed; however, it may be more challenging to
perform and is operator-dependent. Ultrasonography allows for a dynamic examination
of the tendon.


Nonsurgical Management
Acute Achilles tendinopathy is 90% to 95% responsive to nonsurgical management,
which include the use of heel lifts, immobilization, and physical therapy incorporating
eccentric strengthening exercises.19 This exercise regimen has been shown to
successfully increase angiogenesis and healing within the tendon.4,20 The physical
therapy protocol for chronic Achilles tendinopathy involves the use of heavy-load
eccentric strengthening exercises. This protocol has been shown to be comparable to
open débridement of the tendon with regard to pain relief and patient satisfaction.
Limited studies have reported on the success of injectables such as platelet-rich plasma
or sclerosing agents. Although available to patients, insurance companies currently do
not cover the costs of such treatment modalities. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy also
is available. Several studies have shown effectiveness of extracorporeal shockwave
therapy in the management of chronic Achilles tendinopathy.11,12
Surgical Management
Percutaneous Tenotomy
Small, intrasubstance longitudinal incisions proximal and distal to the diseased area
Increases local controlled inflammation and increases circulation
Débridement and Repair
Incise longitudinally within the diseased potion of the tendon (Figure 12)


Surgical Management
Inadequate excision of the diseased tendon will result in poor surgical outcomes and
persistent pain. Excision of the tendon may result in defects requiring addition
procedures, such as V-Y lengthening, central turndown, or FHL tendon transfer to
restore tendon continuity.
For defects smaller than 2 cm, the proximal tendon/muscle belly often can be mobilized
and stretched. An elevator can be used to free proximal adhesions around the
tendon/musculotendinous junction. Tension can be applied to the proximal limb,
promoting creep and allowing for primary repair of the tendon.
V-Y lengthening is performed proximally at the level of the musculotendinous junction.
The increased length achieved is directly related to the angle of the V limbs. A steeper
angle will allow for more length. This is an option for defects ranging from 2 to 4 cm.
Patients have reported satisfactory outcomes but may have persistent plantar flexion
weakness.21 A central turndown flap also can be used for additional augmentation in
patients with a larger defect. A central slip of the proximal tendon is incised and folded
down over the defect, securing this to the distal limb (Figure 14).

FHL tendon transfer should be considered in patients with a large longitudinal defect or
defects involving more than 50% of the tendon thickness. The FHL provides in-phase
firing of the muscle during gait and improved vascularity in the region of the defect
because of the low-lying muscle belly. This tendon can be harvested at the master knot
of Henry in the foot for maximum length or behind the ankle as it passes medial if a
short segment is necessary (Figure 15). A prospective study showed considerable
improvement in functional outcome scores with FHL tendon transfer, with 57% reporting
no great toe weakness.22

Surgical complications associated with FHL harvest include medial plantar nerve
transection and hallux cock-up deformity.23
